title: Superextensive learning in quantum reservoirs at the onset of information scrambling
abstract: The idea that information processing is optimised near the boundary between order and chaos has emerged as a recurring principle across neuroscience, complex systems, and machine learning. Here we test this hypothesis in quantum many-body systems, numerically simulating two-dimensional Ising networks of up to $N=20$ spins, operated as quantum reservoirs for time-series forecasting. Using out-of-time-order correlators (OTOCs), we locate the onset of information scrambling as the input strength is swept, separating regimes where information is frozen and scrambled across the whole reservoir state. We show that prediction precision peaks at the onset of scrambling, along with the number of computational-basis states that the reservoir actively populates. We then show that prediction precision grows as a power law $\sim N^α$ in the reservoir size, superextensively $(α>1)$ at the onset of scrambling and only sublinearly $(α<1)$ in either neighbouring regime. Finally, we show that scrambling enhances the nonlinear components of the reservoir memory while reducing its linear capacity. At the onset, the total memory capacity grows superextensively, provided that the necessary ``forgetting'' mechanism is supplied by a collective relaxation channel. These results consolidate the role of information scrambling in learning systems, turning it from an operating point into a scaling law for the performance of quantum reservoirs.
summary: This work investigates quantum reservoirs, modeled by Ising spin networks, to test if optimal information processing occurs at the boundary between order and chaos. By analyzing information scrambling using OTOCs, the authors demonstrate that prediction performance peaks at this critical onset point. Crucially, they show that the memory capacity scales superextensively at this onset, establishing information scrambling as a fundamental scaling law for quantum machine learning devices.
main_problem: The paper tests the hypothesis that optimal information processing occurs near the boundary between order and chaos, applying this principle to quantum many-body systems used as quantum reservoirs for time-series forecasting.
main_result: Prediction precision peaks precisely at the onset of information scrambling, where the reservoir's memory capacity exhibits superextensive scaling ($\alpha>1$) with system size $N$.
method: The study uses numerical simulations on 2D Ising networks, characterizing dynamics using Out-of-Time-Order Correlators (OTOCs) to locate the scrambling onset, and benchmarking performance via time-series forecasting.
model_or_system: The model is a 2D Ising network of spins, governed by a Hamiltonian involving Ising couplings and transverse fields. The system is operated as a quantum reservoir for time-series prediction, with the control parameter being the ratio $h_x/J$.
key_observables: Prediction precision, Out-of-Time-Order Correlators (OTOCs), Participation Ratio (basis spreading), and Memory Capacity (linear vs. nonlinear).
important_parameters: The critical control parameter is the ratio $h_x/J$, which separates the frozen, onset, and scrambled regimes. Scaling exponents ($\alpha$) are key to quantifying performance.
main_assumptions: The readout mechanism is assumed to be linear (ridge regression), and the reservoir state is reset at each time step to simulate practical constraints.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the time-series prediction protocol, showing the transition from localized (frozen) to global (scrambled) feature population at the onset of scrambling.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical framework by linking information processing optimization to the order-chaos boundary. It then details the simulation protocol using Ising networks and OTOCs to measure scrambling. Finally, it quantifies the scaling laws for prediction precision and memory capacity across the different dynamical regimes.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, scalable physical mechanism (information scrambling) within quantum many-body systems that directly dictates the performance scaling of artificial neural network components, bridging quantum dynamics with machine learning theory.
